Multi-Domain Outcomes
Yuying Lu∗1, Wenbo Fei∗1, Yuanjia Wang†1, and Molei Liu‡2,3
1Department of Biostatistics, Columbia Mailman School of Public Health.
2Department of Biostatistics, Peking University Health Science Center.

Abstract
Precision mental health requires treatment decisions that account for heterogeneous
symptoms reflecting multiple clinical domains. However, existing methods for estimating
individualized treatment effects (ITE) rely on a single summary outcome or a specific set
of observed symptoms or measures, which are sensitive to symptom selection and limit
generalizability to unmeasured yet clinically relevant domains. We propose DRIFT, a
new maximin framework for estimating robust ITEs from high-dimensional item-level
data by leveraging latent factor representations and adversarial learning. DRIFT learns
latent constructs via generalized factor analysis, then constructs an anchored on-target
uncertaintysetthatextrapolatesbeyondtheobservedmeasurestoapproximatethebroader
hyper-population of potential outcomes. By optimizing worst-case performance over this
uncertainty set, DRIFT yields ITEs that are robust to underrepresented or unmeasured
domains. We further show that DRIFT is invariant to admissible reparameterizations of
the latent factors and admits a closed-form maximin solution, with theoretical guarantees
for identification and convergence. In analyses of a randomized controlled trial for major
depressive disorder (EMBARC), DRIFT demonstrates superior performance and improved
generalizability to external multi-domain outcomes, including side effects and self-reported
symptoms not used during training.
Keywords:Precision medicine; Adversarial learning; Item response data; Latent factor model;
Mental disorders.

1 Introduction
1.1 Background
Mental disorders pose challenges for precision medicine due to symptom heterogeneity and
variability in patient responses. Unlike physical illnesses, often defined by clear biomarkers
and objective measurements, the diagnosis of mental disorders relies on a broad spectrum
of subjective symptoms, encompassing mental, cognitive, and somatic factors (Insel and
Cuthbert, 2015). For instance, Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is diagnosed based on nine
core symptoms, which can manifest in over 200 distinct combinations. These diverse symptom
profiles, often complicated by comorbidities, make the development of precise therapeutic
strategies challenging and contribute to the low success rate of first-line treatments, with less
than 50% of patients achieving remission (Gartlehner et al., 2011; McGrath et al., 2020).
One barrier to improving treatment outcomes is the standard practice of relying on a
single clinical summary to guide treatment decision-making. In mental health, treatment
effects often vary across different symptom dimensions, sometimes presenting opposite effects
on distinct domains (Maj et al., 2020). For example, Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors
(SSRIs) effectively alleviate core depressive symptoms but are also associated with side effects
such as sleep disturbances (Ferguson, 2001). Similarly, while antipsychotic medications
may reduce hallucinations in schizophrenia, they frequently cause metabolic side effects,
including significant weight gain and increased diabetes risk (Ballard and Zarate Jr, 2020).
Antipsychotic medications, which may reduce hallucinations and delusions in schizophrenia,
frequently cause metabolic side effects, including significant weight gain and increased diabetes
risk (Tschoner et al., 2007; Marino et al., 2015). Relying on a single summary outcome for
treatment decision-making may improve one symptom domain but harm another. Thus, it is
essential to obtain reliable, generalizable estimates of the treatment effect across multiple
2

outcome domains and latent factors to enable individualized, effective care in mental health.
1.2 Related Literature
Statistical methodology for estimating Individualized Treatment Effects (ITE) has advanced
significantly with the development of machine learning approaches such as causal trees (Athey
and Imbens, 2016), causal forests (Wager and Athey, 2018), and meta-learners (Künzel et al.,
2019; Nie and Wager, 2021; Curth and Van der Schaar, 2021; Kennedy, 2023a). However,
these methods predominantly focus on a single scalar outcome, which is insufficient for the
multifaceted nature of mental disorders.
Whilemultivariateregressioncanincorporatemultipleobservedoutcomes,high-dimensional
and subjective symptom data in psychiatry are more effectively modeled using latent variable
models and factor analysis (Moustaki and Knott, 2000; Muthén, 2002). In this context,
Item Response Theory (IRT) and generalized factor models are widely used to identify
underlying constructs from categorical symptoms (Embretson and Steven, 2000; Reise and
Waller, 2009), with recent advances extending these to high-dimensional settings via joint
maximum likelihood estimation (Chen et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020).
To inform treatment decision-making with multi-domain outcomes, existing approaches
often aggregate sub-domain outcomes into a single global measure using fixed weights. For
instance, recent works have proposed preference-sensitive aggregation (Butler et al., 2018;
Luckett et al., 2021) or composite outcomes (Chen et al., 2020, 2021) to learn individualized
treatment rules. Also, Nwankwo et al. (2024) proposed a reduced-rank multi-objective policy
learning method leveraging low-dimensional representations of the outcomes. However, these
approaches assume a fixed aggregation function, thereby ignoring unobserved or infrequently
observed outcomes that could yield a “worst-case” ITE. This is a critical limitation in
risk-sensitive clinical settings, calling for more generalizable methods (Cinelli et al., 2025).
3

This challenge relates to the growing literature on maximin effects and distributionally
robust learning (DROL), which seeks to optimize performance under the worst-case shift
in data distribution (Meinshausen and Bühlmann, 2015; Sagawa et al., 2019; Wang et al.,
2023, e.g.). While such adversarial learning frameworks have been applied to ITE and policy
learning to address heterogeneity across data sources (Shi et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2024),
they have not been adapted to balance trade-offs across latent symptom domains. These
methods optimize over the convex hull of multiple observed outcomes, which is often overly
conservative and, more importantly, problematic if the measured symptoms are a “biased”
subset of the full symptom spectrum. By restricting optimization to observed items, this
strategy fails to generalize to unmeasured but relevant domains that exist within the full
“hyper-population” of symptoms (see Section 2.5).
1.3 Our Contribution
To address the limitations of using a single outcome for treatment optimization in mental
health, we propose the multi-Domain Robust estimation of Individualized and Factorized
Treatment effect (DRIFT) framework. This approach leverages generalized factor analysis to
identify latent disease constructs from multi-dimensional symptom data and constructs an
“on-target” set of clinically plausible outcomes anchored by a Global Evaluation Outcome
(GEO). By optimizing the worst-case predictive performance across this set, DRIFT ensures
that the estimated treatment effects are stable and balanced across diverse symptom domains.
Our main contributions can be summarized as follows.
Novel Framework:We propose a maximin learning framework that extrapolates the
GEO-anchored uncertainty set in latent space to account for unmeasured or underrepresented
clinical symptoms. Unlike standard group maximin regression methods deterministically
restricted to the empirical convex hull of observed symptom outcomes, this GEO-guided
4

extrapolation renders the solution distributionally robust to variability in observed symptom
coverage. It also yields a more generalizable ITE estimate by recovering the full spectrum
of potential symptoms, thereby protecting DRIFT against failures within clinical domains
underrepresented in the observed data.
Convenient Estimation Procedures with Theoretical Guarantees:We provide a
computationally efficient, three-step algorithm for identifying the optimal treatment effect
estimator. We establish that our maximin problem admits a closed-form solution and prove
the consistency of the resulting estimator. Crucially, we show that our estimator is not
affected by the inherent non-identifiability of latent factor models, remaining invariant to
their rotational indeterminacy.
Enhanced Clinical Generalizability in Real World:We demonstrate the practical
utility of DRIFT through an analysis of the EMBARC (Trivedi et al., 2016) randomized
controlled trial for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). Our results show that DRIFT achieves
superior generalizability to external multi-domain outcomes (e.g., side effects and self-reported
symptoms) not used during model training, highlighting its potential to prevent the neglect
of critical clinical factors.
1.4 Outline of the Paper
We introduce the key concepts and set up the DRIFT framework in Section 2. Based on this,
we develop an estimation method for our proposal in Section 3 and justify its theoretical
properties in Section 4. In Section 5, we conduct extensive simulation studies to evaluate the
finite-sample performance of DRIFT and compare it with existing approaches. In Section 6,
we apply DRIFT to analyze the real-world data collected from a clinical trial studying the
treatment effect heterogeneity of Sertraline on major depressive disorder (MDD). In Section
7, we conclude the paper with a discussion. Technical proofs of the theoretical results and
5

additional numeric results are provided in the Supplementary Material.

2.5 Geometric interpretation of GEO-anchored extrapolation
In clinical practice, the full spectrum of potential symptoms constitutes a “hyper-population”
of outcomes, whereas any given study collects only a subset determined by its design. As
a concrete example, in the clinical trial of major depressive disorder (MDD; Section 6),
mania-related symptoms (e.g., feeling unusually euphoric or energized, talking more than
usual, having a flood of exciting ideas) are not represented in the Hamilton Depression Rating
Scale (HAM-D), a primary outcome in many MDD studies. As a result, ITE estimators
based only on observed outcomes may overlook underrepresented domains and be sensitive
to the particular symptoms included in the study. Interestingly, DRIFT overcomes these
limitations through the GEO-anchored extrapolation strategy. The geometric interpretation
involves two main aspects:
The GEO-anchored setΓ( δ)reduces algorithmic sensitivity:Group maximin
methods (Meinshausen and Bühlmann, 2015) were originally developed for regression on a
common outcome across multiple data sources. In analogy to this strategy, under our setting,
the “observed-only” maximin approach (Obs Maximin) constrains its uncertainty set to the
convex hull of aggregation weights for all the observed factorized outcomes (pink triangle in
Figure 1a). It yields an estimator γobsthat could be highly sensitive to a subset of outcomes
from the hyper-population measured in some specific study. In contrast,DRIFToptimizes
over a GEO-anchored robust regionΓ( δ)that recovers the “hyper-population” of outcomes.
As illustrated in Figure 1a, introducing unobserved weights (e.g., α4andα5) can significantly
13

reshape the convex hull of the observed outcomes’ representation while only mildly perturbing
Γ(δ), yielding a more stable solutionγDRIFT.
Extrapolation enhances generalizability:Confined to the convex hull of observed
outcomes, the observed-only method generalizes poorly to underrepresented or unmeasured
clinical outcomes. For instance, if observed symptoms preferentially load on latent factor
Z2over Z1(Figure 1a), the resulting ITE estimators overlook treatment effects operating
through Z1. Consequently, it fails to detect beneficial effects on unmeasured symptoms or
adverse side effects hidden within underrepresented latent dimensions.DRIFTmitigates
these failures by extrapolating to the larger and more comprehensive “hyper-population”,
thereby accounting for plausible outcomes in underrepresented domains. This yields a more
generalizable characterization of treatment effects. We validate this advantage empirically in
the HAM-D study (Section 6), where the observed-only method suffers from failures in the
underrepresented mania domain, whereasDRIFTmaintains robustness.
We also note that defining the uncertainty set via the excess loss dOensures that our ITE
estimator is invariant to the rotational indeterminacy of the latent factorsZ. The uncertainty
set of theObs Maximinmethod is defined strictly on the coordinates of estimated loadings of
the observed items, which may require more assumptions, e.g. the varimax criterion (Kaiser,
1958), to ensure proper interpretation and identification. Free from this issue, DRIFT remains
well-defined even when the “true” underlyingZis not identifiable (see Proposition 2).

6 Application to EMBARC
6.1 Background of the Study
We appliedDRIFTto a randomized controlled trial of major depressive disorder (MDD),
EMBARC (Trivedi et al., 2016), to assess its real-world performance. Participants were
randomly assigned to receive either sertraline ( A= 1) or placebo ( A= 0). The Clinical
Global Improvement (CGI) scale assessed at the end of treatment was used as the GEO
to guide the construction of the on-target factorized outcome set. Individual items in the
Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAM-D) (Hamilton, 1960), a clinician-administered
depression assessment, were used as the manifest outcomesYto learn latent factorsZ. To
enhance learning efficiency and maintain sample balance, items with few endorsements and
27

inconsistent collection procedures were excluded (van Borkulo et al., 2015; Chekroud et al.,
2017), and sparse categories were combined. Electroencephalogram (EEG) measures of brain
activity related to antidepressant response were also incorporated to improve the estimation
performance on the latent factors (Yang et al., 2024). Because the excess loss for constructing
the on-target set is defined for binary GEO, including representations of continuous EEG
outcomes would lead to scale incompatibility. Therefore, we construct the on-target set using
only HAM-D items and use EEG measures only to improve latent factor estimation. Given
that prior studies identified 2–4 latent factors for depression (Van Dorn et al., 2016; van Loo
et al., 2012; Sunderland et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2021), we fit the factor model with 4 latent
domains. CovariatesXinclude age, sex, Flanker Interference Accuracy score (indicating
cognitive control), and inferred baseline latent domains. After excluding participants with
missing measures, 168 subjects were included in the analysis, of whom 75 received sertraline.
We compared our method with three alternatives:Original GEO,Factorized GEOandObs
Maximin(see Section 5). BecauseObs Maximinsuffers from latent factor non-identifiability,
we applied an oblique promax rotation (Hendrickson and White, 1964) to the loading matrix
and used the rotated structure as the factor estimates for fair comparison. It also improves
clinical interpretability by allowing each rotated factor to better reflect distinct, clinically
meaningful domains. To assess generalizability, we assessed the prediction accuracy (ACC in
Section 5) of each method on external outcomes not used in training. These external outcomes
include (i) the self-reported 17-item Concise Associated Symptom Tracking (CAST) scale, a
validated instrument for quantifying depression-related symptoms by probing experiences
such as anxiety, sleep disturbances, restlessness, and shifts in mood and energy (Minhajuddin
et al., 2020), and (ii) the self-rated Frequency, Intensity, and Burden of Side Effects Rating
(FIBSER) scale, which measures medication side effects (Wisniewski et al., 2006). Because
these outcomes differ clinically from the training responses, performance on them reflects
28

out-of-distribution generalizability.

7 Discussion
The proposed DRIFT framework offers a principled approach to learning robust ITE across
multiple outcome domains, with broad potential applications in precision medicine. Several
extensions could further enhance its utility. First, replacing the explained-variance reward
32

function with an absolute-deviance criterion may reduce conservative estimates for small γ
values and improve robustness to outliers. Second, the current linear treatment response
model for latent factors could be relaxed to incorporate nonlinear CATE models such as
spline regressions, or causal forests (Wager and Athey, 2018). Finally, addressing missing
data in the items is an important extension. Multiple imputation or matrix completion
(Davenport et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2019) can be incorporated.
Another key extension is to directly derive individualized treatment rules (ITRs), using
policy learning or value function optimization (Chen et al., 2021) to guide treatment strategies.
Finally, expanding the framework to handle multiple treatments, including combination
therapies or sequential, multiple assignment randomized trials (SMART) (Lei et al., 2012),
would offer the ability to estimate dynamic treatment regimens.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary: This partial document introduces DRIFT, a new maximin framework for estimating robust individualized treatment effects (ITEs) from high-dimensional item-level data. The framework addresses limitations of existing methods that rely on single summary outcomes or specific observed symptoms, which can be sensitive to selection and lack generalizability to unmeasured clinical domains. DRIFT leverages latent factor representations and adversarial learning to learn latent constructs, construct an anchored uncertainty set that extrapolates beyond observed measures, and optimize worst-case performance to yield ITEs robust to underrepresented or unmeasured domains. The document highlights DRIFT's invariance to reparameterizations, its closed-form maximin solution, and theoretical guarantees. An analysis of a randomized controlled trial for major depressive disorder (EMBARC) demonstrates DRIFT's superior performance and improved generalizability to external multi-domain outcomes. The keywords associated with this work are Precision medicine, Adversarial learning, Item response data, Latent factor model, and Mental disorders.

nodes.title: Our Contribution
nodes.summary: This partial document introduces a novel framework called DRIFT (multi-Domain Robust estimation of Individualized and Factorized Treatment effect) for optimizing treatment effects in mental health. It addresses limitations of existing methods that focus on single outcomes or are overly conservative by optimizing under worst-case data distribution shifts. The framework's main contributions include a novel maximin learning approach that extrapolates uncertainty sets in latent space to account for unmeasured symptoms, providing distributionally robust and generalizable Individualized Treatment Effect (ITE) estimates. It also offers convenient estimation procedures with theoretical guarantees, including a computationally efficient algorithm and proofs of consistency and invariance to latent factor model indeterminacy. Finally, the document highlights DRIFT's enhanced clinical generalizability through an analysis of a Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) clinical trial, demonstrating its ability to generalize to external outcomes not used during training. nodes.title: Outline of the Paper
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes a framework called DRIFT, designed to improve the estimation of individual treatment effects (ITE) by addressing limitations in observed data. Key points include:

*   **Robustness and Generalizability:** DRIFT uses extrapolation to make solutions robust to variability in observed symptom coverage and to recover a fuller spectrum of potential symptoms. This enhances generalizability and protects against failures in underrepresented clinical domains.
*   **Efficient Estimation with Guarantees:** The document outlines a computationally efficient, three-step algorithm for identifying optimal treatment effect estimators. It provides theoretical guarantees, including a closed-form solution for the maximin problem, proof of estimator consistency, and invariance to rotational indeterminacy in latent factor models.
*   **Real-World Clinical Application:** DRIFT's practical utility is demonstrated through an analysis of the EMBARC randomized controlled trial for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). The results show superior generalizability to external outcomes not used in training, highlighting its ability to prevent the neglect of critical clinical factors.
*   **Paper Outline:** The document provides a roadmap of the paper, detailing sections on the DRIFT framework, estimation methods, theoretical properties, simulation studies, real-world application to MDD treatment, and concluding discussions.
*   **Conceptual Framework and Problem Formulation:** It introduces the problem formulation, defining baseline covariates, latent factors underlying mental health, and observed multi-domain symptom measures. It also lays out key assumptions for the model, including measurement conditional independence, measurement invariance, randomized treatment assignment, and the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA).

nodes.title: Factorized outcomes and ITE
nodes.summary:
This partial document introduces a generalized factor model for analyzing outcomes, particularly in the context of precision mental health. Key points covered include:

*   **Generalized Factor Model:** It defines a model where observed outcomes $Y^{(a)}_j$ are conditionally independent given latent factors $Z^{(a)}$, and their conditional expectation is linked to the latent factors via a monotonic function $g_j^{-1}$ and linear coefficients $\alpha_j$ and intercept $\zeta_j$.
*   **Latent Factor Representation:** It defines a class of linear representations of latent factors, $H$, and how to find the "best" latent representation for an observed outcome $Y$ by minimizing expected loss. Different loss functions are suggested for continuous and binary outcomes.
*   **Excess Loss:** A metric called "excess loss" ($d_Y(\phi)$) is introduced to quantify the deviation of a candidate linear representation from a specific outcome. This serves as a distance measure.
*   **Individual Treatment Effect (ITE):** The document defines ITE for a factorized outcome $\phi(Z)$ for a subject with baseline covariates $x$, expressed as the difference in expected factorized outcomes under different treatment conditions.
*   **Global Evaluation Outcome (GEO):** It proposes using a one-dimensional GEO (like the CGI scale) to capture overall intervention effectiveness. A factorized GEO representation ($\phi_{GEO}(z)$) and its corresponding ITE ($\tau_{\phi_{GEO}}(x)$) are defined.
*   **On-Target Set of Factorized Outcomes:** To address the limitations of relying solely on a GEO, it introduces an "on-target set" ($\Phi(\delta)$) of factorized outcomes. This set includes representations that are within a certain deviation ($\delta$) from the GEO representation, allowing for a broader and more balanced characterization of ITE across multiple domains.
*   **Maximin Framework:** A novel maximin framework is proposed for estimating ITE. This framework aims to achieve stable and balanced predictive performance across the range of outcomes in the "on-target set," leading to more generalizable treatment effect evaluations and recommendations. It introduces a reward function ($R_\phi(\tau)$) to measure how well a candidate estimator $\tau(x)$ captures the variation in the ITE function for a given factorized outcome.

nodes.title: Maximin framework
nodes.summary:
The provided document excerpt introduces a novel **maximin framework** for estimating **Individualized Treatment Effects (ITE)**. The core idea is to achieve stable and balanced predictive performance across a range of symptom representations, leading to more generalizable treatment effect evaluations and reliable recommendations.

Key points covered include:

*   **Definition of Aggregation Weights and Uncertainty Sets:** The document defines aggregation weights associated with factorized outcomes and introduces an uncertainty set, denoted as $\Gamma(\delta)$, which expands as $\delta$ increases. This set represents a "latent neighborhood" around a clinical anchor (GEO), capturing a spectrum of relevant, potentially unmeasured, outcomes.
*   **Maximin Framework for ITE Estimation:** A novel maximin framework is proposed to estimate ITE. This framework aims to maximize the worst-case reward function, $R_\phi(\tau)$, which measures how well a candidate estimator $\tau(x)$ captures the variation in the ITE function $\tau_\phi(x)$.
*   **DRIFT Estimator:** The resulting estimator from this maximin optimization is named the **multi-Domain Robust estimator of the Individualized and Factorized Treatment effect (DRIFT)**. It is formulated as an adversarial learning problem seeking a balance between the ITE function and the representation.
*   **Geometric Interpretation and Clinical Relevance:** The document provides a geometric interpretation of the GEO-anchored extrapolation, illustrating how the uncertainty set $\Gamma(\delta)$ in a latent space relates to observed and unobserved clinical outcomes. This approach is clinically relevant as it accounts for unmeasured but important symptom domains, making the treatment effect estimation more robust.
*   **Identification and Computation of DRIFT:** Theorem 1 establishes an explicit-form solution for the DRIFT estimator, showing it can be computed as a weighted combination of latent-factor-wise ITE functions by solving a quadratic programming problem.
*   **Advantages of Using Latent Representations:** The document highlights the advantages of using low-dimensional latent representations ($Z$) over original outcomes ($Y$) for defining the on-target set. This includes invariance to scaling/rotation and overcoming high-dimensionality and measurement noise.
*   **GEO-Anchored Extrapolation:** The GEO-anchored extrapolation strategy is explained as a way to reduce algorithmic sensitivity by optimizing over a robust region $\Gamma(\delta)$ that recovers the "hyper-population" of outcomes, rather than being constrained to the convex hull of observed outcomes.

nodes.title: Geometric interpretation of GEO-anchored extrapolation
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses a method called GEO-anchored extrapolation for analyzing outcomes, particularly in clinical settings. The main points covered are:

*   **Addressing limitations of original outcomes:** The proposed method (GEO-guided on-target factorized outcome subspace) overcomes issues with original outcomes having different distributional types and scales, and is invariant to scaling or rotation. It also effectively handles high-dimensionality and measurement noise.
*   **Geometric interpretation of GEO-anchored extrapolation:**
    *   **Reducing algorithmic sensitivity:** The GEO-anchored set (Γ(δ)) makes algorithms less sensitive to specific subsets of observed outcomes. It contrasts with an "observed-only" maximin approach that is constrained by the convex hull of observed outcomes and can be highly sensitive to study-specific symptom inclusions. DRIFT, by optimizing over a robust region, recovers the "hyper-population" of outcomes and yields a more stable solution.
    *   **Enhancing generalizability:** The method extrapolates to a larger, more comprehensive "hyper-population" of outcomes, accounting for plausible outcomes in underrepresented domains. This improves generalizability compared to methods confined to the convex hull of observed outcomes, which can overlook treatment effects in unmeasured domains. This is illustrated with an example of major depressive disorder (MDD) where mania-related symptoms are not represented in the HAM-D scale.
*   **Invariance to rotational indeterminacy:** The method ensures the ITE estimator is invariant to the rotational indeterminacy of latent factors, unlike methods that rely on estimated loadings of observed items and may require additional assumptions for proper interpretation.
*   **Generalized factor analysis:** The document introduces the setup for generalized factor analysis, where for each subject, baseline covariates, treatment received, and multi-domain outcomes are observed.

structure.title: Estimation Method
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses a method called DRIFT for estimating individual treatment effects (ITE). The main points covered are:

*   **Stability of DRIFT:** DRIFT aims to create a more stable solution by reshaping the convex hull of observed outcomes' representations with minimal perturbation.
*   **Enhanced Generalizability:** Unlike observed-only methods that generalize poorly to underrepresented outcomes, DRIFT extrapolates to a "hyper-population" to account for plausible outcomes in underrepresented domains, leading to more generalizable treatment effect characterizations. *   **Invariance to Latent Factor Indeterminacy:** DRIFT's uncertainty set definition ensures invariance to the rotational indeterminacy of latent factors, unlike methods that rely on specific coordinate definitions and potentially require additional assumptions for interpretation. It sets up the notation for baseline covariates ($x_i$), treatment received ($a_i$), and multi-domain outcomes ($y_i$) for each subject ($i$).

nodes.title: Generalized factor analysis
nodes.summary:
This partial document discusses a method called DRIFT for estimating individual treatment effects (ITE) in a generalized factor analysis framework. The main points covered are:

*   **Improving Stability and Generalizability:** DRIFT aims to create a more stable solution by reshaping the convex hull of observed outcomes' representations. It addresses the poor generalizability of observed-only methods, which are confined to the convex hull of observed data and can miss treatment effects in underrepresented or unmeasured clinical outcomes. DRIFT extrapolates to a "hyper-population" to account for plausible outcomes in these underrepresented domains, leading to more generalizable treatment effect characterizations. This is validated with an example from the HAM-D study.
